extracted.intended_audience: students and contestants preparing for mathematical olympiads / problem-solving competitions
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and principles for analyzing and solving two-player finite impartial games appearing in math contests: how to classify positions, construct winning strategies, detect invariants and periodicities, and apply geometric/tiling/symmetry tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition into losing (L) and winning (W) positions
rubrics_metrics.description: The set P of all positions can be partitioned into the set L of losing and the set W of winning positions: P = L ∪ W, L ∩ W = ∅. A player finding himself in a position in L will lose provided his opponent plays correctly. A player finding herself in a position in W can force a win whatever her opponent does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties and use: From each position in L, every move must result in a position in W. From every position in W, a move to a position in L must be possible. L must contain at least one final position f from which there is no move out. The analysis task is to identify L (the losing positions); once L is known, a player always moves to an L-position and thus forces a win. This is the fundamental classification used throughout the chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairing (matching) strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide the set of all positions into pairs so that there is a legal move from the first element of each pair to the second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Play rule: Whenever the opponent occupies one element of a pair, move to the other element of that pair. If there is a single unpaired position, occupy it initially; otherwise play second. This simple construction guarantees that the opponent runs out of moves first. Use in many contest games to give a short, constructive winning strategy. For more complex games, combine pairing with a precomputed table of losing positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtraction/subtraction-like games: detect modular invariants
rubrics_metrics.description: For subtraction games (take-away games) identify a modular invariant class that characterizes losing positions (e.g., Bachet's Game: L = multiples of k+1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: work modulo (k+1) or relevant modulus: show that from a nonmultiple you can move to a multiple, and from a multiple no legal move reaches another multiple. Examples: Bachet’s Game (moves 1..k) ⇒ L = multiples of k+1. For move-sets that are powers of two, show L are multiples of 3, etc. The general technique is to find a residue class closed under legal moves and then prove optimality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table-of-losing-positions + periodicity detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct the sequence/table of losing positions step-by-step (start small and compute forward) until a pattern or periodicity emerges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this when the move-set is finite but not trivially modular (example: M = {1,3,8}). Translate the game to a board and compute losing positions iteratively until you detect a repeating pattern (periodicity), then prove it holds for all. This method is recommended as a practical playing strategy as well as a proof method for contest problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wythoff’s game: constructive algorithm and Beatty-sequence characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Losing positions [x(n), y(n)] can be constructed by: x(n) is the smallest positive integer not yet used, and y(n) = x(n) + n. The sequences form complementary Beatty sequences related to the golden ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences and proofs: plotting suggests x(n) ≈ t·n, y(n) ≈ (t+1)·n with t = (1+√5)/2. Prove complementarity using Beatty's theorem: if α, β are irrational and 1/α + 1/β = 1 then ⌊α n⌋ and ⌊β n⌋ partition the positive integers. Use the constructive minimal-unused-integer algorithm to generate initial values and then prove the closed forms. This is the standard solution method for Wythoff-like two-pile games.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symmetry (reflective strategy) on boards
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit geometric symmetry: choose/occupy the central symmetry element and thereafter mirror opponent moves across a symmetry axis/point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical application: on symmetric boards (chessboard, polygon diagonals) one player responds to every opponent move by the symmetric move with respect to a chosen symmetry line or center, thereby maintaining symmetry and ensuring a win (or at least tying undesirable options). Examples include knight/bishop placement games and diagonal-drawing games of polygons. If the center is not a lattice point, select an initial move that restores symmetric decomposition, then mirror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domino / tiling pairing strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition the board into 2×1 dominoes; treat each domino as a pair and always respond by moving/placing in the other square of the domino.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application: king/king-move games or placement games where revisiting squares is forbidden. After partitioning into dominoes, if the opponent plays in one square of a domino, move to the paired square; this preserves a winning invariant. Use this to reduce complex board games to simple parity/pairing wins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrow / directed-pair decomposition on movement boards
rubrics_metrics.description: Preplace directed arrows (or pairings of squares) so that legal moves follow arrows; start on an arrow source and follow the arrow chain to trap the opponent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique example (Fig. 13.2): place arrows so that from any square the only legal successor is the arrow's head; start on an arrow source and move along its direction; opponent can only move to arrow sources, allowing you to follow to arrow ends. This constructive decomposition converts complicated move rules into a forced path strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Halving / subset-count argument for minimization problems
rubrics_metrics.description: When repeatedly applying operations that group or split objects, track the number of distinct subsets/classes and use halving (or similar) bounds to establish lower bounds on the number of moves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: one-person chip-reduction problem where boxes with 1..1990 chips are reduced by subtracting the same number from selected subsets; argue that after each move the number of distinct subsets is at least half the prior number, yielding a logarithmic lower bound (11 steps). Then give an explicit sequence achieving the bound. Use partition counts and monotonicity arguments to obtain tight bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity and small-modulus invariant reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce the game to arithmetic modulo a small modulus when only parity or small-residue information matters (e.g., sign-insertion game, parity-taking games).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: sign-placement problem reduces modulo 2 so subtraction = addition; strategy reduces to forcing pattern 0,1,0,1,...; for digit-sum/divisibility games reduce to mod 9 and use complementary replies (e.g., reply with 7−x to force digital sum 7n). General method: identify the minimal modulus capturing the invariant (parity, digital sum mod 9, etc.), then design mirroring/complement strategies in that modular arithmetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forcing a root / sign-change via chosen evaluations (polynomial coefficient games)
rubrics_metrics.description: In games where players assign polynomial coefficients, force a real root by choosing coefficients that guarantee a sign change of the polynomial at two points (intermediate value theorem style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (polynomial x^10 + *x^9 + ... + 1): pick constants µ and c>0 so that for any choice of the last odd-power coefficient the combined polynomial F satisfies cF(1) + F(−2) ≤ 0, which ensures F has a root in [−2,1]. Technique: select evaluation points and linear combinations to bound values and force a sign change; uses continuity/IVT implicitly. This is a construction used to show one player can always secure the existence of a real root.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratio/invariant reduction in Euclid-type subtraction games
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze Euclid-style games by comparing ratios a/b and using moves that reduce the ratio into specific intervals; identify threshold α (often related to (1+√5)/2) separating winning/losing regimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (Euclid game): show that if a ≥ 2b then first player can force a win. More generally find α such that if a > α b first player wins; analyze moves by considering the effect on the ratio and showing existence of moves that map to positions with desired ratio properties. Use number-theoretic/continued-fraction style reasoning to characterize winning regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of complementary Beatty sequences to characterize complementary integer sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When two monotone integer sequences partition the positive integers, characterize them as Beatty sequences ⌊α n⌋, ⌊β n⌋ with 1/α + 1/β = 1 (used to prove complementarity for Wythoff-like sequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application: after observing linear growth numerically, conjecture α,β (often involving the golden ratio), then prove every positive integer appears exactly once using Beatty's theorem. This gives closed formulas for losing-position sequences in certain two-pile impartial games.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial-central-choice and symmetry-restoration when center is not available
rubrics_metrics.description: If the natural symmetry center is not a legal or lattice point, choose an initial move that restores a symmetric decomposition and then apply the symmetry response strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in coloring problems where the geometric center is not a lattice point, first color a specific pivot square so that the remaining board splits into two symmetric parts; thereafter mirror the opponent's moves. This initial step is crucial to enable the pairing/mirroring strategy when perfect central symmetry isn't directly usable.
